summary:
Consensual, private, non-commercial same-sex sexual activity between adults has been lawful in Guatemala since 1871, following earlier Spanish colonial punishment of sodomy.

Guatemala provides no legal gender recognition. Since 2016 a person may change a legal name to match gender identity only with judicial permission; legal gender cannot be changed, and a person cannot self-report gender for official documents, which must show the sex and name assigned at birth. The resulting mismatch between presentation and identity documents exposes a trans visitor to scrutiny during identity checks.

Guatemala is bound by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion OC-24/17 of 9 January 2018, which holds recognition of gender identity on official documents to be a human right under the American Convention on Human Rights and requires states parties to grant same-sex couples access to all existing domestic family registration systems, including marriage with all rights deriving from marriage. Guatemala's compliance with the opinion is not recorded in these sources. A December 2017 bill to recognise the right to gender identity and allow transgender people to change name and gender on birth certificates was rejected in August 2018 by both the Legislative and Constitutional Points Commission and the Women's Commission; a later legislative proposal for a gender identity law has been advocated without enactment.

Legislative action has moved in the opposite direction. Initiative No. 5940, received by the Legislative Directorate on 12 July 2021 and presented to the plenary on 13 September 2021, proposed a law to guarantee the integral protection of children and adolescents against "gender identity disorders". Bill 5490 advanced in December 2021 to remove education regarding transgender individuals in schools on grounds of protecting children and adolescents, and to require censorship of media featuring transgender individuals; it was unanimously approved by the Congress education committee and moved for full congress review. Human Rights Watch reported in January 2022 that bills before the Congress would erase gender-identity protections and restrict legal recognition.

Guatemalan law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or public accommodations such as cafes, restaurants, nightclubs and cinemas. A May 2017 bill proposing to add gender identity to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 as a protected category remains unadopted, and no convictions for discrimination on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds are recorded through 2021. Bias-motivated crimes on the basis of gender identity are reported to be tolerated by the government, especially where harassment or violence is directed at transgender people, with the absence of hate-crime protection attributed to prevailing attitudes about sexual identity and gender roles.

Central American governments have long excluded trans women from femicide protections, and Guatemalan officials have justified this exclusion by stating that transgender women are not "biological women". The exclusion is official and underpins the documented violence context.

Prison placement follows birth sex. A 2020 Human Rights Watch report documents trans women held in men's prisons in Guatemala, facilitating anti-trans violence and exposing them to sexual assault. Bárbara Herrarte, a trans activist with the trans-led organisation Redmmutrans, described her time in a men's prison: "Always, at night, someone got in my bed and forced me to have sex with him." The report records no gender-identity-based placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice, and no court ruling on trans custody.

Conversion practices are documented as continuing. Evangelical-funded conversion therapy centres, mainly in rural areas, subject persons to electroshock therapy, "corrective" rape prosecuted only as rape and not as a hate crime, forced marriage and coerced sex; conversion practices, including by mental health professionals, remain normalised.

There is no legal recognition for same-sex couples as marriage, civil unions or domestic partnerships. A civil unions bill introduced in December 2016 by Deputy Sandra Morán has not been debated since. The Law for the Protection of Life and Family, approved by Congress on 8 March 2022 with a renewed congressional approval recorded on 9 March, would have expressly prohibited same-sex marriage in the Civil Code and required schools to teach heterosexuality as the norm; after President Alejandro Giammattei announced a veto on grounds it violated the Constitution and international agreements, Congress archived and discarded the law on 15 March 2022 with 119 votes, leaving those prohibitions without effect.

United Nations and NGO reports from the late 1990s documented systematic targeting of LGBT people for death as part of a social cleansing campaign, including the 1997 gunning down in Guatemala City of transgender AIDS activist Luis Palencia. The most recent documented fatal case against a trans person in this record is that 1997 killing; no later fatal case is documented. The most recent documented instance of trans-specific violence of any kind in this record is the 2020 prison sexual assault described above.

Official hostility is current. In August 2025 the Guatemalan Congress hosted the Meeting for Religious Freedom, Life and Family to advance an anti-LGBTIQ agenda. Despite the election of a more progressive government in 2024, Congress remained predominantly conservative with no significant pro-LGBTIQ initiatives.
tangentialFactors:
Arcus Foundation reported in May 2024 that the Inter-American Court's 2017 gender-identity opinion advanced legal gender recognition in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, and that a vociferous opposition movement defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash in all four countries. The Guatemalan trajectory sits inside that regional pattern rather than apart from it.

A majority of Guatemalans affiliate with the Catholic Church or Pentecostal churches, and attitudes towards LGBT people tend to reflect prevailing religious mores. Those faiths have traditionally upheld socially conservative attitudes and in particular tend to regard homosexuality and cross-dressing as signs of immorality, a view reflected in the dominant political parties, while most other parties generally ignore LGBT rights.

Openly LGBT political representation began with lesbian Deputy Sandra Morán elected in January 2016 and gay Deputy Aldo Dávila elected in June 2019 on a platform to criminalize hate crimes and hate speech against the LGBT community. Former President Álvaro Colom supported civil unions; President Jimmy Morales supported the ban proposal, stating that Guatemala believes in family based on the marriage of a man and a woman.

Visibility history is limited: only one gay bar was allowed from 1976 until the late 1990s; OASIS was permitted in 1993 to provide HIV/AIDS education and expanded to LGBT rights after the 1996 end of the civil war; the first gay pride parade was held in Guatemala City in 2000. Pre-Spanish Mayan tolerance extended only to ritual homosexual acts by shamans and priests, not to transgender people specifically.

The LGBT organisation Lambda flags forced internal displacement from violence. Raw incident counts for Guatemala are not supplied in these sources, so no ranking against other jurisdictions is possible.
localsOnly:
Residents cannot self-report gender for official government documents, which must show gender and name assigned at birth, causing problems accessing government services such as education and basic resources that require official ID. The judicial permission route to a name change available since 2016 does not extend to legal gender.

Guatemalan law does not prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or public accommodations, and does not prohibit it on the basis of sexual orientation either, except for the 1997 Code on Childhood and Youth safeguarding children and youth from discrimination based on sexual orientation and that of parents, which was repealed in 2003. A May 2017 bill to add sexual orientation to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 is likewise unadopted. The penal code prohibition of discrimination on grounds including gender does not explicitly cover gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics, and no convictions on those grounds are recorded through 2021.

Residents held in the prison system are placed by birth sex with no gender-identity-based placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice and no court ruling on trans custody, exposing trans women in men's prisons to sexual assault as documented in 2020.

Conversion therapy centres operate with social and institutional acceptance, including by mental health professionals, and involve electroshock therapy, forced marriage and coerced sex; "corrective" rape is prosecuted only as rape, not as a hate crime. Attempts to ban educational materials on transgender identities have persisted since at least 2021.

There is no hate-crime protection on the basis of gender identity, and bias-motivated crimes against transgender people are reported to be tolerated by the government.
outOfScopeNotes:
Guatemala's compliance with Inter-American Court advisory opinion OC-24/17 of 9 January 2018 is not recorded in these sources; the opinion binds Guatemala as a state party to the American Convention on Human Rights, but no source documents implementation or refusal.

Whether Bill 5490 of December 2021 or Initiative No. 5940 of 2021 was enacted, stalled or withdrawn after committee stage is unresolved here. The inventory records committee approval and referral only.

No trans-specific violence rate, count or denominator is available for Guatemala in this inventory, so no comparison with the general homicide rate can be made and no magnitude of risk can be stated. The record supplies individual dated incidents only.

Current practice at the border on document markers, entry screening and visa decisions is not sourced. Nothing in the inventory documents differential treatment of trans travellers at Guatemalan ports of entry.

The platform of the government elected in 2024 on gender recognition and the fate of any gender-identity legislation after August 2025 are unresolved in these sources.

Whether courts have ordered or refused name changes under the 2016 procedure, and how frequently, is not sourced.
